summary: Details how SIP uses DNS to turn a SIP URI into the address, port and transport of the next hop, and to let a server find a backup client. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: To call someone you need their address. This explains how the phone system looks up where to send the call, with a backup plan.

what is a naptr record in sip

subtitle: How a SIP client turns a SIP URI into the address, port and transport of the next hop, using DNS NAPTR and SRV records.

tldr.problem: A SIP proxy that wants to forward a call to a user in another domain knows only a URI such as sip:joe@example.com. It needs the IP address, port and transport protocol of a server for that domain, with backups if a server is down.
tldr.mechanism: The client uses DNS: NAPTR records to learn which transports the domain supports and in what order, then SRV records to find servers with priorities and weights, then A or AAAA records for addresses. Servers use the same tools to find a backup when a client has failed.
tldr.outcome: The procedures replace those in RFC 2543 and are a Proposed Standard. RFC 7984 and RFC 8553 later updated this document.

facts.label: Default without hints
facts.value: UDP for SIP URIs, TCP for SIPS URIs

facts.label: Failure triggers
facts.value: 503 response, transport failure, or timeout with no response

today: RFC 3263 is a Proposed Standard and replaces the server-location rules of RFC 2543 (RFC 2543). It has been updated by RFC 7984 and RFC 8553, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: SIP Servers and the Trapezoid
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP, RFC 3261) is a client-server protocol for starting and managing communication sessions. End systems are user agents and intermediate elements are proxy servers. A typical call forms the SIP trapezoid: a caller (UA 1) in domain A talks to proxy 1, which forwards the request to proxy 2 in the domain of the called party (domain B), which forwards it to UA 2.

Proxy 1 has to work out which server to contact for domain B. It does this with DNS, using both SRV and NAPTR records. This RFC describes the exact DNS procedures for that job.
sections.eli5: When you call a friend in another town, your phone company hands the call to their phone company, which rings your friend. The first company has to find out where the second one lives first.

sections.title: Problems DNS Has to Solve
sections.content:
DNS is needed for two things. First, proxy 1 must find the IP address, port and transport protocol of a server in domain B. SIP can run over TCP, UDP and SCTP, and TLS is defined for TCP only, so a client has to discover which transports a domain offers and which it prefers. The client intersects its own list with the server's list and picks the protocol the server prefers.

Second, proxy 2 must be able to find a backup for proxy 1 if proxy 1 fails after forwarding a request, so that a response can still be delivered. This matters in SIP because a human may need to answer, and tens of seconds can pass between a call request and its acceptance.

Other constraints shape the design. Call setup should take no more than a few seconds, so each hop has little time for lookups. Domains need to publish a set of servers with priorities and weights for crude capacity-based load balancing. Because proxies talk to thousands of domains and rarely talk to the same one twice, they cannot keep live availability state. They try servers in some order until one answers and cache the result for a while.
sections.eli5: The caller needs to know which doors the other side has open, and which one they like best. And if the person who started the call disappears, there must be a spare person to pass the answer back to.

sections.title: Choosing a Transport Protocol
sections.content:
The procedures run once per transaction, and apply to a SIP or SIPS URI. The TARGET is the maddr parameter of the URI if present, otherwise the host part. The URI itself is not rewritten; the lookup only yields an address, port and transport.

The client picks the transport in this order:

  • If the URI has a transport parameter, that transport SHOULD be used.
  • If not, and the TARGET is a numeric IP address or an explicit port is given, the client SHOULD use UDP for a SIP URI and TCP for a SIPS URI.
  • Otherwise it SHOULD query NAPTR records for the domain. The relevant service fields are SIP+D2X and SIPS+D2X, where D2U means UDP, D2T means TCP and D2S means SCTP.
  • If no NAPTR records exist, the client does SRV queries for the transports it supports, using _sip for SIP URIs and _sips for SIPS URIs.
  • If no SRV records exist either, it SHOULD use TCP for SIPS and UDP for SIP.

A client resolving a SIPS URI MUST discard services that do not say SIPS. A domain that offers NAPTR records for a server MUST publish at least three: SIP+D2T, SIP+D2U and SIPS+D2T. SIPS records SHOULD sort ahead of SIP records, and a SIPS+D2U record SHOULD NOT be published because TLS cannot run over UDP. For backward compatibility with RFC 2543, a domain MUST also keep SRV records under the original query domain even if the NAPTR replacement points elsewhere.
sections.eli5: First the caller asks which delivery trucks the other side uses and which one they like best. If they do not say, the caller just uses the regular truck.

sections.title: Finding the Port and IP Address
sections.content:
Once the transport is known, the client finds the address and port:

  • A numeric IP address is used as is, with the URI's port or else the default port for the transport.
  • A hostname with an explicit port: look up A or AAAA records and try each address in turn at that port. This differs from RFC 2543, which used SRV records even when the port was 5060.
  • A hostname with no port: run an SRV query on the name from NAPTR processing, or for the chosen transport, following the usage rules of RFC 2782. If there are no SRV records, fall back to A or AAAA at the default port.

RFC 2782 does not say what happens on failure, so this RFC defines it for SIP. Failure means a 503 response, a transport failure (such as a fatal ICMP error for UDP or a failed TCP connection), or a transaction layer timeout with no response at all. The client SHOULD then create a new request, identical except for a new Via branch ID, which makes it a new transaction, and send it to the next element in the list.
sections.eli5: After choosing the truck, the caller looks up the street address. If the first house does not answer, it tries the next one on the list, with a fresh note each time.

sections.title: Stateless Proxies
sections.content:
Once a server has been contacted successfully, all retransmissions of the request, the ACK for non-2xx final responses and any CANCEL MUST go to that same server. That server's identity is transaction state, which is a problem for stateless proxies. If retransmissions spread across servers, each server would create a new dialog, which could ring the same phone several times.

RFC 2782 does not give a deterministic order for records with equal priority, so a stateless proxy MUST define its own, for example by alphabetizing. Domain administrators are RECOMMENDED to give equal-priority SRV records different weights, such as 1000 and 1001. If the first server answers, the proxy can stay stateless. If not, it SHOULD act as a stateful proxy for that transaction. Even then, the RFC admits that DNS TTL expiry mid-transaction can still send retransmissions to different servers, and says this is unavoidable.
sections.eli5: If a helper forgets who they gave the message to, a second copy might go to a different person and your friend's phone rings twice. So they should either remember, or always pick helpers in the same order.

sections.title: Server Usage and Backup URIs
sections.content:
Normally a server sends a response back over the connection the request came in on, or for unreliable transports to the source address and the port in the Via header. If that fails (the connection closes before the response is sent, or the transport reports a fatal error), the server looks at the sent-by value in the topmost Via header:

  • A numeric IP address: send there, using the Via transport and the port in sent-by or the transport's default. A Via transport of TLS means TLS over TCP.
  • A domain name and a port: query A or AAAA records and try each address in turn.
  • A domain name and no port: query SRV records, using _sips if the Via transport is TLS and _sip otherwise, and try the sorted list.

The RFC also covers building URIs for headers such as Contact and Record-Route. A URI such as sip:1.2.3.4 leaves no way to reach a backup if that element fails. A domain name with SRV records, such as sip:server23.provider.com, can have one low-priority-value record pointing to the element itself and further records with higher values pointing to backups.
sections.eli5: If the usual way back is broken, the server looks up a second way to reach the caller. Putting a name instead of a house number on your business card lets you point to a spare house.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NAPTR records let a client discover that a server supports TLS. An attacker who modifies them could push a client to a non-secure transport. The sips URI scheme limits this: it is always sent only over TLS, so an attacker cannot force a bid down by deleting or changing DNS records. At worst they can block communication by deleting all records.

A client that often contacts the same domain SHOULD cache whether the domain's NAPTR records contain SIPS. If SIPS records disappear later, that is a sign of a possible attack, and the client SHOULD raise an alert and MAY reject the request. For SIPS records using a site certificate, both the queried domain and the replacement or SRV target domain MUST be valid under that certificate.

Proxies usually run the NAPTR queries, so a dishonest proxy could ignore SIPS entries. The RFC says little can be done about this, since clients depend on proxies to implement the protocol properly.
sections.eli5: Someone could scribble on the phone book to trick you into using an unlocked door. A locked-door-only address, and remembering what the book said before, help you notice the trick.

sections.title: The NAPTR Service Registry
sections.content:
Section 8 describes the NAPTR usage as the Transport Determination Application of the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS). Its input is the URI, the first rule extracts the host part, the database is DNS, and the output is an SRV record for the server to contact.

IANA maintains a table mapping NAPTR service field values to transport protocols. New entries MAY be added through standards track RFCs under RFC 2434. A registration must give the service field, the protocol (with a reference describing it), and name and contact information. The initial values are SIP+D2T and SIPS+D2T for TCP, SIP+D2U for UDP, and SIP+D2S for SCTP.
sections.eli5: A shared list says which short code means which delivery truck, so everyone reads the phone book the same way.

data.title: Resolving sip:user@example.com
data.code:
;          order pref flags service      regexp  replacement
   IN NAPTR 50   50  "s"  "SIPS+D2T"     ""  _sips._tcp.example.com.
   IN NAPTR 90   50  "s"  "SIP+D2T"      ""  _sip._tcp.example.com
   IN NAPTR 100  50  "s"  "SIP+D2U"      ""  _sip._udp.example.com.

;;          Priority Weight Port   Target
    IN SRV  0        1      5060   server1.example.com
    IN SRV  0        2      5060   server2.example.com
